questions.question: What is 'counting of figures' reasoning primarily about?
options: Measuring the physical size of a diagram
Systematically counting how many valid geometrical figures (of a given type) are hidden within a composite diagram
Drawing new figures from scratch
Only counting the outermost boundary shape
questions.rationale: Counting-of-figures questions ask for the total number of valid figures — of one type or several — hidden within a larger composite diagram.

questions.question: What is the 'basic principle' behind counting figures?
options: Guess a number that looks reasonable
Break a complex figure down into fundamental building blocks and count combinations of them systematically
Only count the largest figure present
Ignore any figure that overlaps with another
questions.rationale: The basic principle is decomposing a complex figure into its fundamental building blocks, then systematically counting valid combinations of those blocks.

questions.question: What does the 'golden rule' of figure counting emphasize?
options: Counting as fast as possible
Never rely on visual counting alone; use a systematic method so no figure is missed or double-counted
Only count squares, never triangles
Always assume the answer is an even number
questions.rationale: The golden rule is to avoid relying on visual scanning alone, since it easily misses hidden or overlapping figures — a systematic method is required for a reliable count.

questions.question: What is the recommended first step in a general figure-counting workflow?
options: Immediately apply a memorized formula
Identify all the basic building-block figures before looking for combined/composite ones
Count only the figure's perimeter
Skip straight to the final answer
questions.rationale: The workflow starts with identifying every basic, undivided figure first, since composite figures are built by combining these basic units.

questions.question: What formula gives the number of distinct line segments formed by n points on a single straight line?
options: 2n
questions.rationale: Each segment is uniquely determined by choosing 2 of the n points as its endpoints, giving the combination formula n(n-1)/2.

questions.question: Using that formula, how many segments do 5 points on a line form?
Why does the n(n-1)/2 line-segment formula work?
options: It doesn't actually work in general
Because each segment is uniquely determined by choosing any 2 of the n points as its endpoints
Because it counts each point twice
Because it only applies when n is even
questions.rationale: This is exactly the 'n choose 2' combinatorial logic: any 2 of the n points determine exactly one unique segment between them.

questions.question: In a grid made of 2x2 unit squares (a 3x3 array of points), how many 1x1 squares exist?
questions.rationale: A 2x2 grid of unit squares contains exactly 4 unit (1x1) squares.

questions.question: In that same 2x2 grid of unit squares, what is the TOTAL number of squares of all sizes (1x1 and 2x2 combined)?
questions.rationale: 4 unit squares plus the 1 larger 2x2 square gives a total of 5 squares.

questions.question: Why is a systematic rule-based approach recommended over just visually scanning a figure to count squares or triangles?
options: Visual scanning is always faster and equally accurate
Visual scanning easily misses combined or overlapping figures, especially as the diagram gets more complex
Rule-based approaches only work for very simple figures
There is no real difference between the two approaches
questions.rationale: As a figure gets more complex, visual scanning becomes increasingly likely to miss combined figures made of several adjacent regions — a systematic method avoids this.
